title: Assessing the Effects of Illuminance and Correlated Color Temperature on Emotional Responses and Lighting Preferences Using Virtual Reality
research_question: How will Preferred Lighting Conditions (PLC) (brightness and color temperature) be affected by Initial Lighting Conditions (ILC)? What influence will the order effect of the presented lighting conditions have on the preferred lighting condition in VR? How will the self-reported level of arousal and emotional valence be affected by given illuminance and CCT of the ILC, and are these effects moderated by gender? How does the lighting preference profile of users in the given virtual environment differ in different lighting conditions?

participants.description: Thirty-three healthy adult participants were recruited, with 6 excluded due to technical problems, resulting in a final sample of 27. Twenty-three were undergraduate university students, with the remainder being graduate students and faculty members. 16 (59%) were female, and 11 (41%) were male. Age ranged from 18–64 years (mean 24.16, SD 8.09). All reported no medical eye problems, no difficulty distinguishing colors, and sufficient sleep (7–9 hours). 59% used eyeglasses (75% for seeing far, 18% for seeing far and close). Most were students/researchers (66.6%) and programmers (25%), with daily tasks including typing (92%), computer use (77%), and reading (62%).
participants.recruitment: convenience methods (word-of-mouth and announcements on departmental e-mail lists)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A contemporary interior office space (3.7 m x 7.2 m x 3.0 m) created in Unreal Engine 4.26 (UE4). Participants experienced the VR environment seated, using a Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display. 17 distinct lighting conditions were simulated using six luminaires, varying in Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) from 1500 K to 7500 K and luminous flux from 300lm to 4500lm (corresponding to 45lx to 780lx illuminance). Conditions included constant illumination with different CCTs, constant CCT with different illumination intensities, and 'quadrant' conditions (Warm-Dark, Cold-Dark, Warm-Bright, Cold-Bright).

mechanisms: Lighting adaptation, habituation, and fatigue in VR could explain the participant's preference for lower illuminance.
The vividness and richness of the light color play a significant role in the level of arousal experienced.
Differences in responses between genders suggest gender-specific impacts on emotional and preference outcomes.
The stimulus range and anchor point employed in the adjustment task substantially impacted the participants' preferred illuminances and CCTs.
Analyzing user control actions provides insights into individual preference profiles.
implementation_implications: Lighting settings have profound implications for creating conducive environments for work or healing.
Understanding user lighting preferences (illuminance, CCT) can inform personalized lighting solutions, enhancing comfort and satisfaction.
Gender-specific design considerations are necessary for more inclusive environmental design.
Awareness of how lighting conditions influence arousal can aid in designing environments that promote productivity, focus, and general wellbeing.
Insights from user adjustment profiles can help optimize lighting design in various contexts.
Designers can use information about user uncertainty patterns to create more intuitive interfaces and lighting systems.

limitations: The range of luminance that VR HMDs can create is still constrained compared to actual light sources, decreasing utility at very high and very low illuminance extremes.
The study did not address the comparison or validation of physical versus virtual illumination modeling.
Current VR systems do not provide great dynamic range compared to the human eye.
Rapidly evolving lighting simulation methods in UE4 may create barriers to generalizing results or comparing them with other game engines.

The study experienced a higher-than-expected attrition rate due to corrupted VR log file data (missing timestamps) and technical difficulties like HMD battery crashes, often caused by researcher error.
The study used a convenience sample primarily of undergraduate students, limiting generalizability.

Demographic variables or other elements such as participant sleep schedules or time of day were not assessed, which may impact preferred illuminance and CCT results, especially given participant diversity.
